newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway premier sets foot down, tired of opposition.
newsitem.headline: Norway premier sets foot down, tired of opposition.

text.p: Thorbjoern Jagland, prime minister of Norway's new Labour minority government, has threatened to resign if the opposition continues to hound his justice minister over a scandal involving the national intelligence service.
Jagland's ultimatum, made in interviews on Wednesday evening, put the deeply divided opposition on the defensive less than a year before a general election.

The Labour Party chairman, who has encountered major difficulties since succeeding veteran premier Gro Harlem Brundtland on October 25, suddenly showed the clout that was the hallmark of his tough predecessor.
"The government will go if parliament touches the justice minister," Jagland told the national news agency NTB.

He accused the opposition of launching another witchhunt, this time for Justice Minister Anne Holt, after forcing Energy Minister Grete Faremo to step down on Monday as a result of the scandal dating back to her spell as justice minister.

Hans Olav Oestgaard, head of the intelligence service, also was forced out of office in the row over the covert surveillance of a prominent left-wing politician assigned to examine the spy organisation's activities.

"If the opposition now continues to attack the justice minister it has not understood how serious the situation is," Jagland told Norwegian television. "We have an intelligence service that is virtually lying down, its back broken.
"I have now contributed by clearing the deck for a new start and I think the others should help out and not continue attacking a justice minister who has been in office for just a few days."
Analysts say the prime minister dumped Faremo to halt a battle with parliament over the intelligence service, but he had shown he would not sacrifice Holt.
Kjellbjoerg Lunde, parliamentary leader of the Socialist Leftist Party (SV) which had pushed for Faremo's resignation, said she was not after Holt.
"There is no talk of a vote of no-confidence in Holt," she said. "We just felt there was a need for her to explain in more detail what she knows."
Holt has been asked to answer questions soon on the scandal before a parliamentary control committee.

Faremo was justice minister when the intelligence service last year started looking into the background of Berge Furre, a member of a parliamentary committee assigned to examine the work of the service.
The scandal surfaced with the release of a declassified document recently and raised the political temperature ahead of the elections in September 1997.

It was the second time in less than three weeks that a minister was forced to resign from Jagland's government, whose main strength is the inability of several opposition parties to present a viable alternative.

National Planning Minister Terje Roed-Larsen, who quit as a U.N.-appointed Middle East mediator to join the new government, resigned on November 27 amid a storm of criticism over alleged wrongdoing in a share-option deal he profited from 10 years ago.
